ci-two-means-claims-s1.title: Noise-canceling headphones and reading scores
ci-two-means-claims-s1.text: Sixty students at a large high school volunteered for a study. They were randomly assigned, 30 to each group, to take a timed reading test (out of 100) with noise-canceling headphones (H) or without them (N), in a noisy room (invented data). Boxplots of both groups show no strong skew or outliers. The school would buy headphones only if they raise the mean score by more than 5 points.

table.caption: Summary of reading scores and a 95% two-sample t interval for $\mu_H - \mu_N$

ci-two-means-claims-s2.title: Apartment rents in two cities
ci-two-means-claims-s2.text: A housing group took independent random samples of one-bedroom apartment listings in cities A and B and compared monthly rents (invented data). Both samples are large and small shares of each city's listings. The 99% two-sample t interval for $\mu_A - \mu_B$, the difference in true mean monthly rent, is shown.

table.caption: The 99% interval for the difference in mean monthly rent

items.q: Does the interval give convincing evidence that headphones raise the mean reading score? Build the justification.

why.correct: The claim is $\mu_H - \mu_N > 0$. Every plausible value in the interval is positive, so 0 (no difference) is not plausible.

options: Because every value in the interval from 0.72 to 8.28 is greater than 0,
Because the headphone group's sample mean is higher,
Because 5 is in the interval,

why.1: A higher sample mean alone could be chance; the interval accounts for chance.
why.2: Whether 5 is inside decides the 5-point question, not whether there is any gain.

options: the interval gives convincing evidence that
the interval proves that
the interval does not give convincing evidence that

why.1: An interval never proves a claim.
why.2: 0 is outside the interval, so a gain is supported.

options: the true mean reading score is higher with headphones than without, for students like these
every student scores higher with headphones
the 30 students with headphones scored higher on average

why.1: The interval is about mean scores; some students may do worse.
why.2: That is already known from the sample; the claim is about the true means.

conclude.model: Because every value in the interval from 0.72 to 8.28 is greater than 0, the interval gives convincing evidence that the true mean reading score is higher with headphones than without, for students like these.

items.q: Can the school conclude that the headphones caused the higher scores?
options: No, because the students who took part were volunteers, not a random sample
No, since a confidence interval by itself is unable to show cause and effect
Yes, for students like these volunteers, because of random assignment
Yes, for each high school student in the country, since the groups were random

why.correct: Random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; random sampling (absent here) would allow generalizing to a larger population.
options: Volunteers limit how far the results generalize, not the causal conclusion for students like them.
Cause and effect comes from the design. With random assignment, an interval can support a causal claim.

Random assignment makes the groups alike on average except for the headphones, so the difference can be credited to them. The volunteers were not a random sample, so generalizing to all students is not justified.
The volunteers were not a random sample of all students.

items.q: Does the interval give convincing evidence that headphones raise the mean score by more than 5 points, the school's threshold?
options: No, because values from 0.72 to 5 are inside the interval
Yes, because the sample difference of 4.5 points is close to the threshold of 5
Yes, because each value in the interval is greater than 0
No, because the interval proves the gain is less than 5

why.correct: A difference can be statistically significant (0 outside the interval) without being shown practically important (more than 5 points).
options: Gains smaller than 5 points are plausible, so the evidence does not show the gain is large enough to matter to the school.
The sample difference is below 5, and smaller true gains are plausible.
That supports some gain, not a gain of more than 5.
Values above 5, up to 8.28, are also plausible; nothing is proven.

items.q: A second analyst subtracts in the other order and reports an interval for $\mu_N - \mu_H$. What interval and conclusion does she get?
options: From 0.72 to 8.28, so students without headphones score higher on average
From $-8.28$ to $-0.72$, with the same conclusion
From $-0.72$ to $-8.28$, so there is no convincing evidence of a difference
From 8.28 to 0.72, and the conclusion now depends on the order used
The parameter changed, so the signs must change too.
Reversing the order flips the signs. Every value is now below 0, which says the no-headphones mean is lower: the same finding.
The ends must be in order (lower first), and 0 is still outside.
The conclusion does not depend on which group is subtracted, and the lower end comes first.

items.q: Does the interval give convincing evidence that mean rents differ between the two cities? Build the justification.

why.correct: 0 is inside the interval, so "no difference" is plausible, along with differences in either direction.

options: Because 0 is in the interval from $-45$ to 130 dollars,
Because the interval is mostly above 0,
Because the interval is wide,

why.1: Only whether 0 is inside matters, not how much of the interval is on each side.
why.2: Width alone does not decide the claim; whether 0 is inside does.

options: the interval does not give convincing evidence that
the interval gives convincing evidence that
the interval proves that

why.1: 0 is a plausible value, so a difference is not established.
why.2: An interval never proves a claim.

options: the true mean monthly rents of one-bedroom listings differ between cities A and B
the sample mean rents differ
the rents of most apartments differ

why.1: The sample means are known; the claim is about the population means.
why.2: The interval is about mean rents, not most apartments.

conclude.model: Because 0 is in the interval from -45 to 130 dollars, the interval does not give convincing evidence that the true mean monthly rents of one-bedroom listings differ between cities A and B.

items.q: A reporter writes, "The study proves that rents are the same in the two cities." What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because 0 is inside the interval from $-45$ to 130
The interval shows city A is more expensive
A 99% interval is too wide to say anything
0 is plausible, but so are differences up to 130 dollars

why.correct: Failing to find convincing evidence of a difference is not evidence of no difference.
options: Being in the interval makes 0 plausible, not proven.
Negative values are in the interval too, so no direction is established.
It says something useful: no convincing evidence of a difference, and how big a difference is plausible.
A plausible value is not a proven one. The interval also allows city A to cost up to 130 dollars more, or city B up to 45 dollars more.

items.q: If the group had built a 95% interval from the same large samples instead, which statement is true? (For large samples, $t^*$ is close to 2.58 for 99% and 1.96 for 95%.)
options: It would be narrower, about $-24$ to 109 dollars, and still contain 0
It would be wider, so it would contain 0 with more room to spare
It would be the same interval, since the data are the same
It would be narrower and would exclude 0, since 95% is less strict

why.correct: Center 42.5 dollars; 95% margin about 66 dollars; interval about $-24$ to 109 dollars, which contains 0. The conclusion does not change.
options: Same center, $\frac{-45 + 130}{2} = 42.5$; the margin shrinks from 87.5 to about $87.5 \times \frac{1.96}{2.58} = 66$, so the interval still reaches below 0.
A lower confidence level gives a narrower interval, not a wider one.
The critical value changes with the confidence level, so the margin changes.
It is narrower, but its lower end, about $-24$, is still below 0.

items.q: What range of differences in mean rent does the interval treat as plausible?
options: From city A costing 45 dollars more to city A costing 130 dollars more
From city B costing 45 dollars more to city A costing 130 dollars more
Differences near the center of 42.5 dollars, and not the ends
Differences in individual rents from $-45$ to 130 dollars

why.correct: $\mu_A - \mu_B$ from $-45$ to 130: B up to 45 dollars more expensive, or A up to 130 dollars more expensive, on average.
options: A negative difference, $\mu_A - \mu_B = -45$, means city B costs more.
Negative values mean B is more expensive on average, positive values mean A is, so the interval covers both directions.
Every value in the interval is plausible, not just the center.
The interval is about the difference in mean rents, not individual apartments.

items.q: Two huge random samples of 20,000 phones each give a 95% interval for the difference in mean battery life (brand X minus brand Y) from 0.03 to 0.09 hours. Which statement is the best summary?
options: The difference is statistically significant but too small to matter
The difference is large, because 0 is not in the interval
There is no difference, because the interval is near 0
The interval is unreliable because the samples are far too large to trust

why.correct: Practical significance asks whether the plausible differences are big enough to matter in context. Here the largest plausible difference is 0.09 hours, about 5 minutes.
options: Every value is above 0, so X lasts longer on average, but by at most about 5 minutes: statistically significant, likely not practically significant.
Excluding 0 shows there is a difference, not that it is large.
The interval excludes 0, so there is convincing evidence of a difference.
Large samples make intervals precise; that is why a tiny difference is detected.

items.q: A 95% interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is from 2.4 to 9.1. What would a two-sided test of $H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$, on the same data, conclude?
options: Fail to reject $H_0$, because the interval is wide
Reject $H_0$ at each significance level, including 0.01 and 0.001
Reject $H_0$: there is convincing evidence that the means differ
An interval and a test answer different questions, so nothing follows

why.correct: Values outside a 95% interval are exactly those a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ rejects.
options: Width does not decide; whether 0 is inside does.
At smaller $\alpha$ the matching interval is wider and might contain 0.
0 is outside the 95% interval, and a 95% interval matches a two-sided test at the 0.05 level.
At matching levels, an interval and a two-sided test agree.

items.q: Independent random samples of 35 phones of brand 1 and 35 of brand 2 give mean battery lives of 11.8 hours ($s = 1.9$) and 10.9 hours ($s = 2.3$). Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$, in hours.

why.correct: $(11.8 - 10.9) \pm 1.997\sqrt{\frac{1.9^2}{35} + \frac{2.3^2}{35}} = 0.9 \pm 1.007$, from $-0.11$ to 1.91 hours ($t^* = 1.997$ at df 65.7; the Table B row for df 60 gives 2.000 and the same interval to two places). On the exam the conservative df 34 is also accepted ($-0.12$ to 1.92). Using $z^* = 1.96$ ($-0.09$ to 1.89) is wrong, because the standard deviations are estimated.

items.q: The 95% interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ (brand 1 minus brand 2 battery life) is from $-0.11$ to 1.91 hours. Does it give convincing evidence that brand 1 lasts longer on average?

why.correct: 0 is inside the interval, so a mean difference of zero is plausible and brand 1 being better on average is not established.

options: Because 0 is in the interval from $-0.11$ to 1.91 hours,
Because most of the interval is above 0,
Because the sample mean for brand 1 is higher,

why.1: The share of the interval above 0 does not matter; 0 is still plausible.
why.2: A higher sample mean can happen by chance.

options: the interval does not give convincing evidence that
the interval gives convincing evidence that
the interval proves that

why.1: 0 is plausible, so the claim is not established.
why.2: An interval never proves a claim.

options: the true mean battery life of brand 1 phones is greater than that of brand 2 phones
the 35 brand 1 phones lasted longer on average
every brand 1 phone lasts longer than every brand 2 phone

why.1: That is known from the sample; the claim is about the true means.
why.2: The interval is about means, not individual phones.

conclude.model: Because 0 is in the interval from -0.11 to 1.91 hours, the interval does not give convincing evidence that the true mean battery life of brand 1 phones is greater than that of brand 2 phones.

items.q: From the headphones experiment (95% interval for $\mu_H - \mu_N$ from 0.72 to 8.28 points), which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.
options: A true mean gain of 3 points is plausible
Headphones cause higher mean scores for students like these
A true mean gain of 10 points is plausible
There is a 95% probability that the true gain is between 0.72 and 8.28
95% of students score between 0.72 and 8.28 points higher with headphones

why.correct: Plausible values are those in the interval; random assignment supports a causal reading; confidence is about the method.
options: Right: 3 is inside the interval.
Right: random assignment and 0 outside the interval support it.
10 is above 8.28, outside the interval.
The 95% describes the method, not a probability for this interval.
The interval is about the difference in means, not individual students.

items.q: A student builds separate 95% t intervals for two groups' means. They overlap slightly, so she concludes there is no convincing evidence of a difference. What is the problem?
options: Nothing is wrong, since overlap means 0 is in the interval for the difference
Overlap can hide a real difference; estimate $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ directly
She should have used 99% intervals
Overlap proves the means are equal

why.correct: The standard error of a difference, $\sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}$, is smaller than $\text{SE}_1 + \text{SE}_2$, so judging by overlap is too cautious.
options: Overlap does not translate directly into 0 being inside the interval for the difference.
Two intervals that overlap a little can still give a two-sample interval that excludes 0. The difference needs its own standard error.
The level is not the issue; comparing two separate intervals is.
Nothing about intervals proves equality.

items.q: A 90% interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ contains 0. What can you say about the 95% interval from the same data?
options: It does not contain 0
It may or may not contain 0
It gives convincing evidence of a difference
It also contains 0

why.correct: Same center, larger $t^*$: the 95% interval contains the 90% interval.
options: A wider interval around the same center keeps every value the narrower one had.
Here the answer is certain: wider intervals contain the narrower ones.
0 is inside it, so it does not.
The 95% interval has the same center and is wider, so it covers the whole 90% interval, including 0.

items.q: In a randomized experiment, the 95% interval for the true mean weight loss on diet A minus diet B is from 0.4 to 1.1 kilograms over a year. A doctor considers 3 kilograms the smallest change worth a patient's effort. Which statement fits?
options: Diet A works better on average, but not by an important amount
The diets are equally effective, because the interval is close to 0
Diet A is clearly worth recommending, because 0 is outside the interval
Nothing can be said, since 3 is outside the interval

why.correct: Statistical significance: 0 is outside. Practical significance: the plausible differences, at most 1.1 kilograms, are well below 3.
options: Every value is above 0, so diet A gives more loss on average; every value is also far below 3 kilograms.
0 is outside the interval, so there is convincing evidence of a difference.
Statistical significance alone does not make the difference large enough to matter.
Knowing 3 is outside is useful: gains that large are not plausible.
